feedback: If the marker is placed short of 1 for 4/4: lay the four quarter pieces end to end — they fill exactly one whole with nothing missing and nothing left over, so 4/4 sits exactly on 1, not before it.
If 8/4 is read as 'eight' or as separate digits: count the quarters as you stack — it takes four to reach 1 and four more to reach 2, so 8/4 lands on 2.
Prompt: 'How many quarters do you need to make exactly one whole? What fraction is that?' to reinforce b/b = 1.
activities.intendedInsight: A fraction can land exactly on a whole number: four quarters compose one whole, so 4/4 IS 1, and 8/4 IS 2. This happens whenever the numerator is a multiple of the denominator.
learnerActions: Starting from 0 on a number line, add one quarter piece at a time and read the running total: 1/4, 2/4, 3/4 …
As the fourth quarter is added, check where the marker lands and name the fraction there (4/4) and the whole number at that point (1).
Keep stacking quarters past one whole and find where 8/4 lands (on 2), noticing it took eight quarters — two full wholes' worth.
Say in your own words how many quarters make exactly one whole, and complete b/b = 1 for quarters (4/4 = 1).
activities.title: Iterate quarters until a fraction lands on a whole number

feedback: If a denominator of 1 seems meaningless or like zero: a cut into 1 piece leaves the whole intact, so 5/1 is five whole, uncut bars — not nothing.
If the child cannot write 5 as a fraction: ask how many pieces each whole is cut into when it is left whole (one), then the numerator counts the wholes: 5/1.
Check placement: 5/1 should sit on the 5 mark, confirming 5/1 = 5.
activities.intendedInsight: A denominator of 1 is meaningful: it says the whole has not been cut, so n/1 is simply n wholes. Every whole number can be written as a fraction.
learnerActions: Work with whole, uncut bars and read a denominator of 1 as 'the whole is left in one piece'.
Write the number 5 as a fraction (5/1) and explain that it means five wholes, each uncut.
Place 5/1 on a number line at 5, and 3/1 at 3, checking they land on the whole-number marks.
Explain what the bottom number 1 is telling you when you write 3 = 3/1.
activities.title: A denominator of 1 means 'not cut': writing whole numbers as fractions

feedback: If 5/2 is called a whole number 'because 5 and 2 are both whole numbers': 5 ÷ 2 is not exact — 5 is not a multiple of 2 — so 5/2 lands at 2½, between the whole numbers, not on one.
If 6/3 is mishandled: 6 ÷ 3 = 2 exactly, and three thirds make one whole so six thirds make two wholes; 6/3 lands on 2.
Prompt: 'Is 5/2 a whole number? Where does it land, and what does that tell you?'
activities.intendedInsight: A fraction equals a whole number exactly when the numerator is a multiple of the denominator; a/b can be read as a ÷ b. Having both digits be whole numbers (as in 5/2) does not make the fraction a whole number.
learnerActions: Decide for each of 6/3, 8/4 and 5/2 whether it equals a whole number, and sort them into 'equals a whole number' vs 'not'.
For each, test whether the numerator is a multiple of the denominator, using division: 6 ÷ 3 = 2, 8 ÷ 4 = 2, 5 ÷ 2 is not a whole number.
Place 5/2 on a number line to show it lands at 2½, between 2 and 3.
Match 8/4 to the whole number 2 and explain how you knew.
activities.title: Sort fractions: whole number or not?

feedback: If the prediction was 'before 1' because 'a fraction is always less than one': the four quarters fill exactly one whole with nothing left over, landing on 1 — so a fraction CAN equal a whole number.
Confirm the generalisation: this works whenever the numerator is a multiple of the denominator (4/4, 8/4, 6/3), not just for this one case.
If the reason given before observing was correct, ask the child to predict where 8/4 lands to extend the rule.
activities.intendedInsight: Stating a reason before observing surfaces the belief 'fractions are always parts less than one'; building four quarters that fill exactly one whole and land on 1 contradicts it.
learnerActions: Before doing anything, PREDICT with a reason whether 4/4 lands before 1, exactly on 1, or past 1 on a number line, and state your reason out loud or in writing first.
Then iterate four 1/4-jumps from 0 (or build four quarters) and observe where you land.
Compare what happened to your prediction, and revise your reason if needed.
State the general rule you now believe about whether a fraction can equal a whole number.
activities.title: Predict-then-check: where does 4/4 land?
